newsitem.title: USA: Source of hepatitis in U.S. school food not found.
newsitem.headline: Source of hepatitis in U.S. school food not found.

text.p: Federal researchers have been unable to determine how frozen strawberries became contaminated with hepatitis that made 300 schoolchildren sick this year, a Senate hearing was told Thursday.
"The source of contamination is not known and may never be known," Health Secretary Donna Shalala said in a letter released at the Agriculture Committee hearing.

"The investigation (by the Atlanta-based Centres for Disease Control and Prevention) did not identify a single event, food handler or contaminated water source of the contamination of the strawberries. The CDC analysis suggests that the contamination occurred prior to the arrival of the frozen strawberries in Michigan."

Processor Andrew and Williamson Sales Co Inc, of San Diego, California, sold the frozen strawberries to the Agriculture Department for distribution in the school lunch programme. Suspect lots were shipped to six states, Michigan, Arizona, California, Georgia, Iowa and Tennessee.
Acting Agriculture Undersecretary Mary Ann Keefe said evidence indicated the strawberries came from Mexico despite rules that only U.S. food was allowed in the lunch programme.
Keefe said the circumstances of how the strawberries were misidentified were "still currently under review. It has not been concluded."
About 250 schoolchildren, most of them in Michigan, were diagnosed with hepatitis A after eating frozen strawberries supplied by the San Diego firm.
Shalala said there was no test at present to detect hepatitis A in fruit. U.S. scientists are trying to develop one.

During the hearing, Representative Nick Smith, Michigan Republican, said he had asked Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin to approve a proposed rule to require the country of origin of frozen food to appear on the front panel of packages.
